rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: Nobody has measured whether you have a sharp spot in your eye, or how sharply you see. In the saltwater crocodile, a relative in another genus, the sharpest vision lies along a streak that runs across the eye from the nose side to the rear side. That crocodile sees at best about 9 cycles a degree, about a third of the 30 a human sees.
rows.note: Both figures are from saltwater crocodile only; the 9 is not carried to alligators because acuity travels only within a genus.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are an American alligator, your cones hold four kinds of visual pigment, where a human has three. One of them senses green light best. The saltwater crocodile, a relative that has been measured, has three kinds of single cone, sensitive to violet, green and red.
rows.note: Left out the 535 nm figure because it has no comparison job; the human count of three is general knowledge, not from a record.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: The pupil in your eye is a narrow upright slit. If you are an American alligator, this is recorded for your species, and for the saltwater crocodile, whose slit pupil is described as mobile. If you are a Chinese alligator, you very likely have the same shape as your relative the American alligator, and for most other crocodiles and caimans nobody has recorded it.
rows.note: Mobility of the pupil is stated only for the saltwater crocodile (R3), so I did not carry it to alligators.

rows.title: Field of view, sharpness, dim light and depth
rows.text: Nobody has measured how much of the world your eyes cover, how sharply you see, how faint a light you can sense, or how you judge depth. A reflecting layer at the back of the eye, called a tapetum, has been found in the common caiman and the saltwater crocodile, and the caiman's retina is adapted to dim light. In the saltwater crocodile the sharpest vision measured is about 9 cycles a degree, against about 30 for a human, and that figure belongs to that species alone.
rows.note: Left out R4 (six crocodilian species, severely defocused underwater) because it does not name the alligator and optics only carry within a genus.
